lessons.title: Radioactivity and the decay law

lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the nature, ionising power and penetration of α, β and γ radiation and write balanced nuclear equations
Use the decay law A = λN, N = N₀e^(−λt) and t½ = ln 2/λ
Apply half-life ideas to radiocarbon dating, medical tracers and safety
reviewNotes: Half-life of carbon-14: 5730 years (often rounded to 5700 or 5600 in textbooks) — check the board's value.
β⁺ decay, electron capture and the neutrino are only mentioned; check the syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Nuclear radiation
blocks.md:
A nuclide ᴬ_Z X has Z protons and A − Z neutrons. Unstable nuclei decay **randomly** (the decay of any one nucleus cannot be predicted) and **spontaneously** (unaffected by temperature or chemistry).

**α**: helium nucleus ⁴₂He, strongly ionising, stopped by paper. **β⁻**: fast electron (from n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino), stopped by a few mm of aluminium. **γ**: photon, weakly ionising, reduced by thick lead. In equations the **total A and Z are conserved**.

blocks.title: The decay law
blocks.md:
The **activity** A = −dN/dt = **λN**, where λ is the **decay constant** (s⁻¹); the unit of activity is the becquerel (Bq = 1 s⁻¹). Solving: **N = N₀e^(−λt)** and A = A₀e^(−λt).

The **half-life** t½ is the time for N (or A) to halve: **t½ = ln 2/λ = 0.693/λ**. After n half-lives the fraction left is (½)ⁿ.

blocks.caption: Radioactive decay: the number of nuclei halves every half-life (here 5 days).
blocks.alt: A decaying exponential curve from 100 per cent with red points at 50 per cent after 5 days, 25 per cent after 10 days and 12.5 per cent after 15 days.

blocks.title: Applications and safety
blocks.md: **Radiocarbon dating**: living things take in carbon-14 from the atmosphere at a steady proportion; after death it decays (half-life about 5730 years) so the remaining activity gives the age. **Tracers** with short half-lives are used in medicine. **Safety**: keep exposure short, distance large and use shielding; handle sources with tongs; stored in lead-lined containers. A Geiger counter's count rate must be corrected for **background radiation**.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the half-life in years with λ in s⁻¹ without converting.
- Saying that after two half-lives all the nuclei have decayed (¼ remain).
- Forgetting to subtract the background count rate.
- Thinking radioactivity can be switched off or changed by heating: it cannot.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Using half-life
blocks.statement: A source has half-life 8.0 days and an initial activity of 6.4 × 10⁵ Bq. Find the decay constant, the activity after 24 days, and the initial number of radioactive nuclei.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Carbon dating
blocks.statement: A wooden object has 60 % of the carbon-14 activity per gram of living wood. Estimate its age (half-life 5730 years).

objectives: Define mass defect and binding energy and use E = Δmc² with 1 u = 931.5 MeV
Describe the binding energy per nucleon curve and explain why fission and fusion release energy

reviewNotes: Nuclear and atomic masses are textbook values given to six decimal places; check them against the board's data sheet.
Binding energy values per nucleon in the bar chart are standard rounded values (²H 1.11, ⁴He 7.07, ¹²C 7.68, ⁵⁶Fe 8.79, ²³⁵U 7.59 MeV).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Mass defect and binding energy
blocks.md:
The mass of a nucleus is **less** than the total mass of its separate nucleons. This **mass defect** is Δm = Zm_p + (A − Z)m_n − m_nucleus. The **binding energy** is the energy needed to separate the nucleus completely into nucleons: **E = Δmc²**.

Useful: 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and **1 u ≡ 931.5 MeV** (using E = mc²).

blocks.title: Binding energy per nucleon
blocks.md:
The **binding energy per nucleon** (E_b/A) measures nuclear stability. It rises steeply for light nuclei, has a broad maximum (about 8.8 MeV) near iron-56, and falls slowly for heavy nuclei.

**Fission** of a heavy nucleus (e.g. U-235 splitting after absorbing a neutron into two medium nuclei and 2–3 neutrons) and **fusion** of light nuclei (e.g. deuterium + tritium → helium-4 + neutron) both move to higher E_b/A, so energy is released.

blocks.caption: Binding energy per nucleon for selected nuclei: the maximum is near iron-56.
blocks.alt: A bar chart of binding energy per nucleon for hydrogen-2, helium-4, carbon-12, iron-56 and uranium-235, with iron the tallest.

blocks.title: Reactions and reactors
blocks.md: In a reaction, energy released Q = (total mass before − total mass after) × 931.5 MeV/u. A **chain reaction** occurs when the neutrons released cause further fission; in a reactor a **moderator** slows neutrons, **control rods** absorb them and a coolant removes heat. Fusion needs very high temperatures and pressures to overcome electrostatic repulsion (as in stars). One U-235 fission gives about 200 MeV.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the mass of the neutral atom with nuclear masses without care (the electron masses cancel only if you use atomic masses consistently).
- Forgetting to convert u to MeV (× 931.5) or MeV to joules (× 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J).
- Confusing the binding energy with the energy released: binding energy is **needed** to break up the nucleus.
- Saying the products have less mass because mass is 'destroyed': it is converted to energy.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Helium-4
blocks.statement: Find the binding energy and binding energy per nucleon of ⁴He. (m_p = 1.007276 u, m_n = 1.008665 u, nuclear mass of ⁴He = 4.001506 u.)
blocks.answer: 28.3 MeV in total; 7.07 MeV per nucleon

blocks.title: Example 2 — Fusion
blocks.statement: Find the energy released in ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n (atomic masses: ²H 2.014102 u, ³H 3.016049 u, ⁴He 4.002603 u, n 1.008665 u).
